title: Food, stories and community records
provenance: Original fictional practice commissioned for this curriculum; not authentic IELTS, not standardised or score-calibrated. No third-party text or diagrams used.

word_count_method: Regex word tokens including hyphenated forms; excludes speaker labels, titles, question text and Q locators.

tasks.task: Future continuous first listen, including planned part pauses
Submit first answers and confidence, without a second play
Four Q-located intensive segments, 15 minutes each

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Welcome to the neighbourhood food festival office. Are you enquiring about a stall for your organisation?

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Yes, our community kitchen has made bread for local events before, and we want to try a public stall. We discussed selling cakes as well, but we cannot organise two production teams this time.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: So I should enter bread as your main product?

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Please do. We can describe how we make it while people look around, although we won't run a cooking demonstration. Our kitchen is across town, and transporting the equipment would be much harder than bringing the finished products.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Which date were you hoping for? Our programme covers two weekends, and the stall arrangements are separate for each one.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: I originally wrote down June the twelfth, because that appeared in an early message. Then our volunteers checked their availability. The nineteenth of June is the date that everyone can manage.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Yes, the twelfth was a provisional date for a smaller event. The nineteenth is available, and I'll put you on that list.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Thank you. I'd rather join once with a full team than attempt both weekends and leave one person trying to manage everything alone.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: How many people will need stallholder passes? Visitors can enter freely, but the setup area is restricted before the festival opens.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: We have six volunteers involved in the kitchen, though not all of them will attend. Two will finish the baking and stay behind, so we'll need four passes.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Four it is. Will the same people be present all day?

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Yes. They'll take turns having breaks without bringing extra helpers into the stall.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: That makes things straightforward. Please let me know in advance if a named person changes, so we can update the entrance list.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: What time should we arrive with our boxes?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Vehicle unloading starts at eight, but your allocated slot is eight thirty. Each row has its own slot to prevent the narrow entrance becoming blocked.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Could we arrive at eight and wait?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: There isn't a waiting area for vehicles at the gate. Please plan around eight thirty, then move the vehicle to the public car park when you've unloaded. The public opening is much later, so you'll still have plenty of time to arrange the stall.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Good. I'll put the unloading time on our transport sheet, not the opening time.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Is there a charge for the stall? Someone told me community groups could apply for a reduced rate.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: They can, and your group meets the conditions. The standard amount is sixty pounds, but your fee will be forty pounds. That covers the stall space and the basic table.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Is that per volunteer?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: No, it's the total for your stall for the day.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: That's helpful. We have a small budget for printing our information sheet, so I'll record forty pounds as the stall cost and keep the printing expense separate when we discuss the budget with the group.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: The last practical question concerns your sign. We provide a table, but groups bring their own display materials.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: We can make a board with our kitchen's name. How do we attach it?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Please bring clips. String tends to hang loose in the shared walkway, and tape can damage the table surface when people remove it.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Clips, then. I'll ask our volunteer to pack them with the board rather than in the food boxes.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Excellent. Keeping the display equipment together will make unloading easier, particularly if a different volunteer has to do that job on the morning.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: We'd like visitors to hear the story behind the kitchen. Should we schedule a long talk at the stall?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: For your location, brief conversations will work better. The walkway needs to stay open, and people may only have a minute before they move on. A short illustrated sheet gives them something to take away if they're interested.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: So the main reason for that sheet is to let people continue reading afterwards?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Exactly. It isn't a substitute for the required stall information, and printing more pages doesn't give a group priority in the programme. Keep the story clear and manageable.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: A friend offered to share our space and sell pottery. It would make the table look attractive, but it's a different organisation.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Please ask them to apply separately. We need to know who is responsible for each stall and what each group intends to bring. You cannot add another seller informally on the morning.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Even if they only use one corner?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Yes. We can consider placing the two groups near each other, although that depends on available space. A separate application is the first step.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: I'll explain that we shouldn't promise them part of our table before they've spoken to you.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: If we sell everything before the end, can we pack up immediately?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: You can stop selling, of course, but please keep your information display open until the agreed closing time. Vehicles cannot enter the stall rows while visitors are still moving around them.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: So we could talk about the kitchen after the products are gone?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: That's ideal. Bring a sign saying you've sold out, and visitors can still find out what your organisation does. You won't need to invent extra activities.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Fine. We'll plan a quieter final hour instead of assuming we can drive away as soon as the last item sells.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: How will you confirm the final stall position?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'll send a numbered site plan with your booking confirmation. Please check the number against the name on the plan; the rough sketch on our website is only an early overview.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Should I call every week to see whether it's changed?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: No need. If your position changes after confirmation, we'll contact you directly and send a revised plan.

turns.speaker: Stallholder
turns.text: Then I'll distribute the confirmed version to our volunteers and replace it if you send an update.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Exactly. That prevents different members of the same team arriving with different versions and searching in opposite directions.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: Before you leave the briefing, look at the map of the festival grounds. North is at the top, and the public entrance is on the southern edge. The stage is the central landmark. The eight lettered areas are separate activity spaces around it. First, the tasting tent is directly north of the stage. It is not the area to the north-east, even though the two can look close together on a small screen. Visitors entering from the south can use the stage as a reference point. Please describe this location by direction rather than by the colour of the tent, because covers may be changed.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: The drinking-water point is in the south-west area. On the map that means below and to the left of the central stage. An earlier layout placed it immediately south of the stage, near the entrance, but that created a crowd where people were arriving. We moved it sideways to give visitors room to stop. The water point remains easy to reach without crossing the performance space. If someone asks for it, make sure you don't simply direct them back towards the entrance. The southern lettered area has another use today, and a visitor following that vague instruction would miss the water station.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: The information and first-aid tent is in the north-east corner of the activity ring. Its shared front desk handles general requests and directs visitors to the appropriate member of staff. Some volunteers remember an arrangement in which the information point stood west of the stage. That was last year's plan, so please use today's map. The north-east position is above and to the right of the stage when you hold the page upright. We use a single shared front desk so visitors do not have to decide which team they need before asking for assistance. Staff inside will help them find the right person.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: The story corner is directly west of the stage, level with its centre. It is a small seated area where contributors can describe their community projects. Please distinguish it from the north-west area, which is reserved for another purpose. We tested the story corner beside the main entrance, but short talks were difficult to hear over the arriving crowd. Moving it to the west gives it a clearer boundary. It still isn't a private interview room, so documentary teams should arrange separate conversations if they need quiet recordings. For an ordinary visitor looking for the programme of stories, however, this western area is the correct destination.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: Finally, the recycling point is south-east of the stage. That is the lower-right area of the map, and it is separate from the drinking-water point on the opposite side. Volunteers will help visitors read the labels on the containers. We haven't placed recycling directly beside the stage because the space there must remain open during performances. Do not send people to the south-west area simply because you remember that another service is located there. Water is south-west; recycling is south-east. Those two locations are the most commonly confused, so use both the direction and the central stage when explaining the route to a visitor.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: The programme has several short performances, with a pause between each one. Those pauses are deliberate. They give visitors time to move between activities and allow the next group to check its equipment without rushing. We haven't introduced them because performers are expected to arrive late. Nor are they extra sales periods that stallholders must fill with announcements. During a pause, volunteers should keep the main paths clear and answer ordinary questions. If a performance starts a few minutes later than printed, consult the stage coordinator before making an announcement. A guessed explanation can spread quickly and leave different parts of the site giving contradictory information.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: Anyone collecting photographs or recorded stories for the festival archive must follow the contributor arrangements. Being at a public event does not mean someone has agreed to a close interview for our archive. Explain the intended use, ask the person, and record their decision using the project form. A general crowd photograph and an identifiable personal story are different tasks in our workflow. If somebody declines, thank them and move on. Do not ask a neighbouring volunteer to approach the same person again. Our aim is to collect contributions people understand and choose to make, not to obtain a particular number of recordings by the end of the afternoon.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: The festival tokens used in the activity trail are not money. Children collect a stamp at participating activities and can show the completed card at the exit desk. Stallholders should not accept the stamps as payment or promise that a completed card wins a purchase. We designed the trail to encourage visitors to explore different community groups, including activities that do not sell anything. A family can take part without buying food or products. If a card is lost, the exit team can explain the available options. Individual volunteers should avoid inventing replacement rules, because inconsistent promises create problems for families who have followed the printed instructions.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: A change to a scheduled story session should be reported to the programme desk first. The desk updates the main noticeboard and tells the volunteers near the affected area. Posting a message on one group's personal social account is not enough, because many visitors will not see it. Equally, crossing out a time on one small sign leaves other copies unchanged. The programme desk provides one coordinated route for revisions. You can help by giving the session name, original time and proposed change clearly. Please wait for confirmation before directing a group to a new location; that space may already be booked for somebody else's activity.

turns.speaker: Festival coordinator
turns.text: At the end of your shift, leave a short handover for the next volunteer. Include unresolved requests and any confirmed programme changes relevant to your position. A long description of every pleasant conversation is unnecessary, although you are welcome to share those stories later. The useful question is what the next person needs to know to do the job. If there is nothing unresolved, say so explicitly instead of leaving the form blank. A blank can mean either no issue or a forgotten handover. Keep personal information out of the public-facing copy and use the staff process for any details that need restricted access.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Let's settle the opening of your student documentary.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: I want a short visual montage of people setting up stalls. It establishes the place before we hear explanations.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: The pictures are attractive, but I'd start with one contributor speaking. Otherwise viewers might not know what question the film is exploring.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: We can add the question as a title, and I still favour the montage.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Would a shorter version bring you together?

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: No, my preference remains a spoken opening.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: Then we should record that we disagree. I support the visual montage, even if the final editing decision goes another way.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What about recording informal conversations without approaching people first?

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: I initially thought hidden recording might make the dialogue sound more natural.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: It would also leave contributors unaware of how their words could be used. I don't support it.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: Having looked at our project requirements, I've changed my mind. We should explain the recording and ask people to participate.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: So hidden recording is no longer a proposal either of you supports?

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: Correct. I withdraw it rather than simply postponing it.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: And I remain against it. We can capture relaxed conversation with willing contributors instead of concealing what we're doing.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: How will you check whether viewers follow the structure?

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: We could show a short pilot clip to classmates who haven't visited the festival.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: I worried that would waste time before the full edit, but a pilot could reveal a missing explanation early. I support testing one now.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: I'd ask viewers to describe the sequence in their own words, rather than just say whether they like it.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: That seems manageable.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: Yes, as long as the pilot is short, I agree with the proposal. We needn't wait until the soundtrack and every transition are polished before finding out whether the basic story makes sense.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: One interview has long pauses. Will you keep it?

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: I want to retain that quiet interview. The contributor describes a difficult first year, and the pauses give the answer room to develop.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: I understand the value, but in this short film I'd replace it with a more concise account.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: We can trim repetition without losing the measured pace. I still support keeping the interview.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Mira, has that suggestion changed your position?

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: No. I would use another speaker and preserve this recording in the project archive. It deserves to be heard, but I don't favour including it in our final short film.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: You have contributions from several groups. How will you track their agreed uses?

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: A source and permission log would connect every clip to the contributor's decision.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: I support that. I originally imagined filenames would be enough, but they cannot tell us whether someone agreed to a classroom screening only.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: We should check the log before exporting each version.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: And if the intended audience changes?

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: We review the agreement rather than assuming permission extends automatically.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: Exactly. So we both want the log, with a clear entry for each source, even if some entries need further discussion before we can use the material.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Your draft compares the same stall at opening and closing.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: I'd show the images in a split-screen comparison. Viewers could see the changed arrangement at once.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: I prefer showing one image and then the other, with a short explanation. Two moving pictures compete for attention.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: We could use still frames, but I still favour the split-screen.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Would still frames resolve your objection, Ethan?

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: They would help, but I remain against that format for this sequence. I want viewers to focus on each image separately.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: Then my support stays, and his doesn't. We'll test both versions before making the editing decision.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: You have space for two more clips in the middle section. Which one is already agreed?

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: The interview with the first-time stallholder who changed her view of the event. At the start she expected only sales, but afterwards she talks about meeting possible volunteers.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: Yes, that change gives the film a clear development. We both selected it.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What about the local celebrity's promotional greeting?

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: It attracts attention, but it doesn't advance our question.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: And the anonymous cheering shot has no clear context. We haven't selected either of those. The first agreed addition is the stallholder describing how her expectation changed.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: And your second agreed addition?

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: The recycling volunteer explaining the sorting process. We have clear images of the labelled containers to accompany that explanation.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: Agreed. It shows work that visitors may overlook, and the volunteer approved the intended screening.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: There is also the close recording of a child discussing the activity trail.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: We don't have the necessary project agreement for that contribution, so it is not one of our selected clips.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: We won't try to fill the gap with an unclear crowd sound either. Our two additions are the changed expectation from the stallholder and the volunteer's explanation of sorting.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Let's finish with captions. The test viewers struggled with the preview.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: Several said the letters were too small on the classroom display. I suggest increasing the font size across all captions.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: I agree. Enlarging just the first caption would leave the same problem elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Did anyone request a more decorative typeface?

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: One classmate liked that idea aesthetically, but it wouldn't address the reading problem, and we haven't adopted it.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: Nor are we planning to animate each line. The first confirmed change is a larger font, with enough space around it to keep the words separate from the image details.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the other confirmed caption change?

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: Consistent speaker labels. In the current edit, one person is introduced by name, another by role, and a third has no label.

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: We should use the same pattern for every contributor, subject to the name each person has agreed to show.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Would removing every label simplify matters?

turns.speaker: Ethan
turns.text: It would remove useful context, so we rejected that.

turns.speaker: Mira
turns.text: We also rejected shortening the display time simply to make the film feel faster. The two changes we've approved are increasing the font size and using consistent speaker labels. We'll check them in a new preview before declaring the captions finished.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: This lecture uses an invented archive project to explore historical market records. The team wants to compare the quantities of selected goods sold at a small market over several years. Its first task is to define a question. Without that step, researchers can spend weeks copying figures that do not help their investigation. A broad interest in local life needs to become a question specific enough to guide selection. Here, the team asks how recorded quantities changed, rather than trying to describe every aspect of the market. That choice will shape which records it copies, how it groups entries and what its eventual conclusions can reasonably cover.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Next, the team records the date attached to each entry. The position of a page in a bound volume is useful, but it is not a reliable substitute for a date. Pages may have been inserted later or grouped by seller rather than by time. If the date cannot be read, the team marks that uncertainty instead of borrowing the date from a neighbouring entry. Clear dates allow observations to be ordered and compared across the chosen period. The original written form is preserved beside the working version, so another reader can check how the researchers interpreted an unusual abbreviation or an incomplete entry.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The third stage is to standardise the units used for quantities. One page might count individual containers while another records a measure of weight. The team cannot simply add the figures because both happen to be numbers. It first establishes what each unit means in the relevant records and whether a justified conversion is available. When no reliable conversion can be made, the values remain separate. Standardising units is therefore not a licence to invent missing information. It is a documented process that makes comparable observations comparable while keeping genuine differences visible. The conversion rule, when used, is stored with the working data rather than only in a researcher's memory.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fourth stage checks for duplicates. An entry may appear in a daily sheet and then again in a weekly summary. Counting both as separate sales would inflate the total. Researchers compare dates, descriptions and other recorded features before deciding that two entries refer to the same event. Similar quantities alone are not enough, because different sales can have equal amounts. A duplicate flag preserves the relationship between the records without destroying the original transcription. The working total includes the event once, while a reviewer can still trace both written appearances. This is a careful checking stage, not an instruction to delete every line that resembles an earlier one.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fifth stage links each working entry to its source. A page reference and archive identifier let another researcher find the original material. Even a beautifully organised table loses much of its value if nobody can discover where a figure came from. The source link also helps when a later reader proposes a different interpretation of handwriting. Researchers can return to the evidence instead of arguing only from copied numbers. In this project the link is stored for every entry, including entries excluded from the final comparison. Exclusion is a research decision that needs an explanation; it should not erase the route back to the material on which that decision was based.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: During analysis, the team must distinguish a blank from a zero. A zero explicitly records that none of the relevant goods were counted. A blank may mean that the information was omitted, the page was damaged, or the category was not used on that occasion. Replacing every blank with zero would turn missing information into a confident statement about activity. The team therefore uses a separate missing-value label and describes the rule in its notes. This does not solve the historical uncertainty, but it prevents a spreadsheet operation from hiding it. Readers should be able to see both the calculated results and the limits of the observations behind them.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Prices and quantities must also remain distinct. A rise in the money recorded for a product does not by itself show that a greater quantity was sold. The price per unit may have changed, or the way payments were recorded may differ. For the question this team has chosen, quantities are the main comparison. Money values can provide context when the records support it, but they cannot silently replace the required measurements. A graph with a clear title and unit label helps prevent that substitution. Researchers should ask what each axis actually represents before treating the shape of a line as evidence for a broader story about the market.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Another issue is coverage. Suppose the surviving records describe only some sellers. Their combined totals would not automatically represent the whole market. The team examines who appears in the documents and whether that group changes across the years. A new seller entering the records can make a total rise even if existing sellers have not changed their activity. Coverage is therefore part of the interpretation, rather than a minor detail reserved for a final footnote. The researchers might restrict a comparison to a consistent subset, while clearly explaining what that subset excludes. Such a choice narrows the claim, but makes the relationship between the evidence and the claim easier to assess.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Some handwritten numbers allow more than one plausible reading. Rather than quietly choosing the value that produces the smoothest graph, the team can calculate a range of possible totals using the defensible alternatives. That range shows how much the uncertain entry could affect the result. It is not a claim that every number between the endpoints was actually observed. The original ambiguity remains documented alongside the calculation. If the broad pattern changes when a single unclear digit is read differently, the final explanation should say so. A precise-looking total is not useful when its apparent precision conceals a choice that readers would reasonably want to examine.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The final report combines the result with an account of uncertainty. It explains which entries were included, how units were treated, where records were missing and which readings remained doubtful. This is not an optional apology after the interesting part of the project. It helps readers decide what the comparison can support and what further evidence would be valuable. The team may still identify a convincing pattern within its defined collection. It simply avoids extending that pattern to every seller or every year without support. A successful report lets another person follow the reasoning from source entries to conclusion, including the points where the available material limits the conclusion.
